newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. fed funds rate of 6.0 pct likely.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. fed funds rate of 6.0 pct likely.

text.p: Economists disagree on how much further the Federal Reserve will tighten U.S. monetary policy in 1997, but most saw the federal funds rate rising to 6.0 percent before the year is out, a Reuters survey showed.

Analysts in the quarterly poll said the difference between the fed funds rate and real short-term interest rates was much narrower now than in 1994, making the Fed's corrective action much less pronounced.

"Given the right set of ingredients -- and we may see them next week -- you can make the case that we'll see 6.0 percent this year," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Flanagan said the big difference between 1997 and the last cycle of tightenings in 1994 was that the Fed was now dealing with a much stronger labor market, incomes were higher and the savings rate was higher due to the wealth effect of a roaring stock market.
"It's truly surprising we haven't seen inflation. But hats off; they called it right," Flanagan said in a reference to that fact that no Fed action was taken earlier.

Next week will see critical data on labor market strength in the quarterly Employment Cost Index and the monthly nonfarm payrolls report. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has voiced concern about wage inflation and strong readings were seen virtually guaranteeing another tightening at the Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meeting on May 20.

"We see a funds rate of 6.0 percent near-term if growth doesn't slow. Greenspan didn't suggest to us he needed to do as aggressive a tightening as in 1994," said Astrid Adolfson, first vice president and an economist at MCM Moneywatch Inc.

Adolfson said 25 basis points would probably be sufficient to accomplish the Fed's goal of cooling economic growth. She expected incremental moves of 25 basis points at a time because that has been the pattern of the Fed under Greenspan.
Scott Pardee, chairman of Yamaichi International (America) Inc, saw the funds rate topping out at 6.0 percent with the Fed moving on both May 20 and July 2.
Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said the Fed would need to move only one more time before its tightening need was completed.
"We see 5.75 percent as the top, but so much is contingent on the data," Stephansen said.

Paul Kasriel, economist at Northern Trust, said the Fed could hold off on any action at its May meeting but would tighten again in July. He expected to see a fed funds rate of 6.0 percent before yearend, however.
